author: ViceTechnicolour
body:
Recently, a lot of maps have been following one quality that is not of preference for many; using complicated names as the title of their map. I feel this needs to be addressed because while I'm not taking a hit on other languages and their translations, we want players to easily recognize maps and not guess what the word actually means or have to play it 10 times to remember. The maps that are complicated also usually have no quality to remember it by due to their concept (Most may be DTM or TDM), and it's really difficult even for myself to remember what maps are which.

For example, a map like "Aqua Dune" represents that the map has water and sand mixed in, but with creativity. Aqua is symbolic for water, and due to the map using wavy sand patterns and terrain condensed across the top and bottom, it's called "Aqua Dune".

For example, a map like "Candyland" represents that the map is composed of candy elements and is simple, to the point. It is easily recognizable as the candy map and the name is attractive instead of a naming process by opening google translate and using fancy latin words. What you see is what you get.

For example, a map like "Dust Devils" represents that the map is sandy and seems to be resembling of a dusty, barren area with very unique terrain and map content/placement. The blocks used are recognizable for a "Dust Devil" and for the map itself, it's become commonly known and popular; a good map is a good introduction.

Right now, here is some examples of "complicated names" on the front page of Map Releases;
Aeternum
Empio
Adoras
Cetacea
Vultus
Arbol
Ascarin

When a lot of maps are like this, you don't want to open /rot and see all these confusing and unrecognizable names. If you gave me a paper right now to show what each map had, I wouldn't be able to answer it. It's not benefiting the server, only causing confusion and potentially making players be uninterested in your map. Interesting names aren't the key to success, but it's not the key to failure either. It's just not helping.

Thanks, ParaSpider

So, what you're saying is that you want map names to resemble words that most common English-speaking people can easily recognize without difficulty, unless its reasonably justified (as in the case of Quintus)?

However, in that respect, Arbol isn't that bad. The map creator does justify it similar to your justification of Quintus, by saying, quite simply, Arbol = Spanish Word for Tree.
